David is using imperative forms, but these communicate a polite request rather than commands. If the imperative form does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use forms in your language that communicate polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please incline your ear to me; please rescue me quickly; please be for me a rocky summit of refuge]

Here David is using the term **ear** to mean hearing or attention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Listen and respond to me] or [Pay attention to me]

Here David is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a **rocky summit** used as a **refuge** and as if he were actually a place that had **strongholds** where he could hide and be safe from his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [be for me like a rocky summit of refuge, and like a dwelling place of strongholds]

David is using these possessive forms, **a rocky summit of refuge** and **a dwelling place of strongholds**, to describe places that are characterized by providing refuge and strength. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive forms for this, you could express these ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [be for me a rocky summit that provides refuge, a stronghold in which to dwell]

nt: Here David is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a large **rock** and a **stronghold** to which he could flee to be safe from his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [you are like a rock that I can flee to for safety and like a stronghold in which I can be safe]
David is using the term **name** to refer to God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as in the UST.

The terms **lead** and **guide** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [direct me]

Here the Hebrew verbs that the ULT translates as **you lead me and guide me** could be: (1) expressing a general truth that has been part of David’s ongoing experience. If you decide this is the meaning, then you can translate the two verbs in this phrase in a similar way to the ULT. (2) expressing something that will happen in the future. Alternate translation: [you will lead me and guide me] or (3) a request that is a prayer to Yahweh. (This option is less likely since David does not use the imperative forms of these verbs as would be expected if these verbs were meant to be requests.) Alternate translation: [lead me and guide me] or [please lead me and guide me]

The implication is that David wants God to lead and guide him so that his enemies do not harm him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you lead me and guide me so that my enemies do not harm me]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [For my life comes to an end with sorrow, yes, my years with groaning; my strength fails from my iniquity, indeed, my bones waste away]

By **For my life has come to an end with sorrow**, David means that his life is being consumed or shortened by grief and distress. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [For my life is being consumed by sorrow] or [For sorrow is shortening my life]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sorrow**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [sorrowfully]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because I have sinned] or [because of the wrong things I have done]

David is using one part of his body, his **bones**, to represent his entire physical being as it deteriorates. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my entire body wastes away]

nt: The expression **I have been forgotten** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People have forgotten me]

David is making a comparison between himself and **a dead man out of mind**. The point of this comparison is that just as a dead man is completely forgotten by people, so David feels that he has been completely forgotten. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I have been completely forgotten, just as people forget about the dead]

David is using **out of mind** as a common expression of the culture to mean “completely forgotten.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is completely forgotten] or [whom people have completely forgotten]

Here David is comparing himself to **a broken vessel** using the word **like**. The point of this comparison is that just as a broken vessel is useless and discarded, so David feels useless and discarded by others. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I am useless like a broken vessel] or [I am discarded like a broken vessel]

x.KJV: Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy presence from the pride of man: thou shalt keep them secretly in a pavilion from the strife of tongues.
x.YLT: Thou hast wrought for those trusting in Thee, Before sons of men. Thou hidest them in the secret place of Thy presence, From artifices of man, Thou concealest them in a tabernacle, From the strife of tongues.

nt: תַּסְתִּירֵ֤⁠ם ׀ בְּ⁠סֵ֥תֶר פָּנֶי⁠ךָ֮ מֵֽ⁠רֻכְסֵ֫י אִ֥ישׁ תִּצְפְּנֵ֥⁠ם בְּ⁠סֻכָּ֗ה מֵ⁠רִ֥יב לְשֹׁנֽוֹת

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [You hide them in the safety of your presence, protecting them from those who plot against them and from cruel words]

Here David is speaking of **the hiding-place of your presence** as if it were a physical shelter where Yahweh could hide people from danger. David means that Yahweh protects people by his divine presence and power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You protect them by your presence from the plots of man]

David is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language as in the UST.

Here David is speaking of God’s protection and help as if it were a physical **shelter** in which God would hide righteous people from the accusatory words of evil people. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [you protect them from people who attack with their words as if you were hiding them in a shelter]

Here, **tongues** represents people speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from people who accuse them with their words] or [from verbal attacks]

x.ASV: Blessed be Jehovah; For he hath showed me his marvellous lovingkindness in a strong city.
x.Darby: Blessed be Jehovah; for he hath shewn me wondrously his loving-kindness in a strong city.
x.KJV: Blessed be the Lord: for he hath shewed me his marvellous kindness in a strong city.
x.YLT: Blessed is Jehovah, For He hath made marvellous His kindness To me in a city of bulwarks.

nt: The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I bless Yahweh] or [Let me praise Yahweh]
בָּר֥וּךְ יְהוָ֑ה כִּ֥י הִפְלִ֘יא חַסְדּ֥⁠וֹ לִ֝֗⁠י בְּ⁠עִ֣יר מָצֽוֹר

David is giving the reason that Yahweh should be blessed after stating that he should be blessed. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because he has shown marvelously his covenant faithfulness to me in a besieged city, blessed be Yahweh]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all the ways he is faithful to his covenant]

The expression **in a besieged city** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is his enemies. Alternate translation: [in a city that my enemies had surrounded]

x.Darby: As for me, I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes; nevertheless thou heardest the voice of my supplications when I cried unto thee.
x.KJV: For I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes: nevertheless thou heardest the voice of my supplications when I cried unto thee.
x.YLT: And I--I have said in my haste, `I have been cut off from before Thine eyes,' But Thou hast heard the voice of my supplications, In my crying unto Thee.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **alarm**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when I was alarmed]

Here, **eyes** represents God’s attention or awareness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I am cut off from your attention] or [you are no longer watching over me]

David uses the words **But indeed** here to indicate a contrast between his fearful thoughts and God’s actual response. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However] or [Yet]
Here, **voice** represents the pleas themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as in the UST.

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [when I cried out to you, you heard the voice of my pleas]

x.ASV: Oh love Jehovah, all ye his saints: Jehovah preserveth the faithful, And plentifully rewardeth him that dealeth proudly.
x.Darby: Love Jehovah, all ye his saints. Jehovah preserveth the faithful, and plentifully requiteth the proud doer.
x.KJV: O love the Lord, all ye his saints: for the Lord preserveth the faithful, and plentifully rewardeth the proud doer.
x.YLT: Love Jehovah, all ye His saints, Jehovah is keeping the faithful, And recompensing abundantly a proud doer.

nt: David is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [faithful people] or [those who are faithful]

x.ASV: Be strong, and let your heart take courage, All ye that hope in Jehovah.
x.Darby: Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all ye that hope in Jehovah.
x.KJV: Be of good courage, and he shall strengthen your heart, all ye that hope in the Lord.
x.YLT: Be strong, and He strengtheneth your heart, All ye who are waiting for Jehovah!

nt: David is using **Be firm** as a common expression of the culture to mean “be strong.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.
The word **your** is plural here because David is speaking to **all the ones waiting for Yahweh**. Use the plural form in your language if your language marks that distinction.
Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and feelings exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

David assumes that readers will know that here **waiting** refers to waiting on Yahweh to help them. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [all the ones waiting for Yahweh to help you]
